question: What kind of men does Moses ask for to share with him the burden of judging the people, and what instructions does he give them?
How does Moses recall the refusal at Kadesh-barnea, and what image does he use in v. 31 for God's care in the wilderness?
The verb עָלָה (‘alah, “go up”) marks the command to go up, the refusal and then the stubborn ascent: what does this sequence show about obedience and the right time?
“Do not be intimidated by anyone, for judgment belongs to God”: in what situation are you tempted to judge someone by size or position?
What instructions does the LORD give about the sons of Esau and about Moab, and why must Israel not take their land?
What role do the notes about the ancient peoples who lived in those lands before play in the middle of the account?
What does it mean that God also gave lands as a יְרֻשָּׁה (yerushah, “possession”) to Esau, to Moab and to the Ammonites?
V. 7 recalls that God knew Israel was journeying “through this vast wilderness”: looking back, where do you notice this care in your own crossing?
Who was Og, and what does the text say about his kingdom, his cities and his iron bed?
Why does God not grant Moses' request, and what does He give him instead of what he asked for?
The verb עָבַר (‘avar, “cross over”) marks Moses' desire and the answer he receives: what does the chapter show about who will cross the Jordan and who will not?
Moses is told to encourage and strengthen Joshua: whom could you prepare and encourage to carry on something you will not finish?
What did the people see and hear at Horeb, and what did they not see?
According to vv. 6-8, what would make the other nations recognize Israel as “a great nation”?
What link does the chapter make between the תְּמוּנָה (temunah, “form”) Israel did not see at Horeb and the images it must not make?
“You will find Him if you seek Him with all your heart”: what would it mean for you to seek God this way, even when far away or in distress?
How do the people react to the voice speaking from the midst of the fire, and what do they ask of Moses?
Why does Moses say the covenant was not made “with our fathers,” but “with all of us who are alive here today”?
In Exodus the Sabbath recalls creation; here, the exodus from Egypt: what does this link add to the meaning of the שַׁבָּת (shabbat, “rest”)?
“Oh, that they had such a heart”: what does this desire of God reveal, and how does it echo in you?
In what places and at what times of day were God's words to be present in the life of the family?
The imperative שְׁמַע (shema‘, “hear”) gives its name to this central prayer of Judaism: what does hearing mean here, beyond listening with the ears?
What relationship does the text establish between the statement that “the LORD is One” and the call to love God with all one's heart, soul and strength?
Why can receiving houses, cisterns and vineyards “you did not plant” become a danger to the people's memory?
When the son asks “What is the meaning of the testimonies?”, the answer begins with a story: what story would you tell to explain your faith?
What must Israel do with the nations of Canaan, with marriages and with their altars?
What reason does the text give for the choice of Israel, and what reason does it rule out?
What does the concept expressed by the verb חָרַם (charam, “devote to destruction”) mean, and how should we read the texts that command it today?
In the face of greater nations, the guidance is to remember what God has already done: what memory helps you face what seems bigger than you?
For what purposes, according to v. 2, did God lead the people through the wilderness, and what did not wear out during those forty years?
What does it mean that “man does not live on bread alone,” and why was this lesson taught precisely with the manna?
Under what circumstances, according to the chapter, does the שָׁכַח (shakhach, “forget”) of God happen?
“My power and the strength of my hand have made this wealth for me”: in what achievements of yours do you run the risk of thinking this way?
What does Moses do when he comes down from the mountain and sees the molten calf?
Why does Moses insist three times that Israel does not receive the land “because of your righteousness”?
What episodes does the chapter gather under the verb קָצַף (qatsaf, “provoke to anger”), and what does this list mean to teach?
Moses intercedes by appealing to the promise to the patriarchs and to God's reputation: for whom could you intercede, even knowing that person's mistakes?
What does God tell Moses to do after the first tablets were broken, and where are the new ones kept?
What does it mean to circumcise “the foreskin of your hearts”?
Why does the memory of having been foreigners in Egypt ground the love for the גֵּר (ger, “foreigner”)?
“What does the LORD your God ask of you?”: how would you sum up, in the words of vv. 12-13, what God asks of you today?
How is the land of Canaan compared with Egypt regarding water and farming?
What is the meaning of setting the blessing and the curse before the people, and enacting them on two mountains on entering the land?
Why does dependence on the מָטָר (matar, “rain”) make faithfulness to God a concrete matter in the new land?
The words were to be talked about “when you sit at home and when you walk along the road”: at what ordinary moments of your day could faith enter the conversation?
Where was Israel to bring its offerings, and what was it to do there with its family?
What does the criticism of “everyone doing whatever is right in his own eyes” mean, and why is it linked to entering into rest?
Why could דָּם (dam, “blood”) not be eaten, and what reason does v. 23 give for it?
“Be careful not to neglect the Levite”: who near you depends on the generosity of others to live?
What criterion does the text give for evaluating a prophet or dreamer whose sign actually comes to pass?
How should we read today such harsh laws against those who entice to idolatry, even when it is a close relative?
Why does a מוֹפֵת (mofet, “wonder”) by itself not prove that someone speaks on God's behalf?
Before acting against a city, one had to investigate and inquire “thoroughly”: how do you check a rumor before believing it and passing it on?
What features make it possible to identify the animals and fish that could be eaten?
What link does the text make between being “sons of the LORD,” “a holy people” and the rules about mourning and food?
The adjective קָדוֹשׁ (qadosh, “holy”) opens and closes the list of foods: what does this frame suggest about the meaning of these rules?
The tithe of the third year fed the Levite, the foreigner, the orphan and the widow: how can your resources reach those who have “no portion or inheritance”?
What happened to debts at the end of every seven years, and who was outside this rule?
V. 4 says there will be no poor, and v. 11 that “there will never cease to be poor”: how do these two statements relate?
What does the שְׁמִטָּה (shemittah, “release”) of the seventh year reveal about the way the Law saw debt and freedom?
The freed servant was not to go out “empty-handed”: how can you help someone start again with dignity?
What are the three feasts at which every man was to appear before the LORD?
Why is the unleavened bread called “the bread of affliction,” and what was it meant to help remember?
What does the repetition “justice, justice you shall pursue,” with the word צֶדֶק (tsedeq), add to the instructions about judges?
The feasts included servants, Levites, foreigners, orphans and widows: who is usually left out of your celebrations?
How many witnesses are required for a death sentence, and what is their role in the execution?
What limits does the text set on the king regarding horses, wives and wealth, and why would each one be dangerous?
Why should the king write for himself a copy of the תּוֹרָה (torah, “law, instruction”) and read it all the days of his life?
The daily reading served “so that his heart is not lifted up above his brothers”: what helps you not to put yourself above others when you have some authority?
What practices does the text forbid the people on entering the land?
Who would be the “Prophet” like Moses, and how has this promise been read in Judaism and in Christianity (Acts 3:22)?
What criterion does the chapter give for recognizing the נָבִיא (navi', “prophet”) who speaks without having been sent?
“You must be blameless before the LORD your God”: in what areas of your life do you seek security or answers outside of God?
What concrete example of accidental death does the text give, and why was the road to the cities of refuge to be prepared?
How does the punishment of the false witness work, and what role does the formula “eye for eye” play here, in a court?
Why does the law require more than one עֵד (‘ed, “witness”) for any offense?
Do not move your neighbor's boundary stone: what limits and rights of others are you tempted to push a little toward your side?
Who is excused from battle, and why?
What difference does the text make between distant cities and the cities of Canaan, and how should we read these laws of war today?
What does it mean that, before fighting a city, Israel was to offer it שָׁלוֹם (shalom, “peace”)?
Even in war the fruit trees were to be spared: what care for creation does this detail inspire in you?
What must the elders do when a body is found in the field and no one knows who killed him?
Why could the body of the one hanged not remain overnight on the tree, and how is this text taken up in Galatians 3:13?
What protection does the law give to the בְּכוֹר (bekhor, “firstborn”) who is the son of the “unloved” wife?
The law on the captive woman requires a month of mourning and forbids selling her: how do you protect the dignity of those in a fragile position before you?
What must the Israelite do on finding a brother's lost or fallen animal?
What difference does the text make between what happens in the city and in the countryside, and what does v. 27 say in the young woman's favor?
What attitude does the verb עָלַם (‘alam, “hide oneself, pretend not to see”) forbid in the face of a neighbor's need?
The parapet on the roof would keep someone from falling: what “parapets” do you need to build to protect those who live with you?
What difference does the text make between Ammonites and Moabites on one side and Edomites and Egyptians on the other?
Why was Israel not to return a runaway slave to his master, and what does this law suggest about his dignity?
Why was it forbidden to charge נֶשֶׁךְ (neshekh, “interest”) to a fellow Israelite?
“Be careful to fulfill what comes from your lips”: is there a promise you made easily and have not yet kept?
What rules protect the poor person who has left a pledge?
What does “each one will die for his own sin” mean, and how is this idea taken up in Ezekiel 18?
Why does the אַלְמָנָה (’almanah, “widow”) appear alongside the foreigner and the orphan, and what does the harvest left behind do for them?
Wages were to be paid “each day”: how do you treat those who work for you or serve you?
What must the brother-in-law do when his brother dies without a son, and what happens if he refuses?
Why is the number of lashes limited, and what does the text suggest by recalling that the guilty one is “your brother”?
The weights were stones: what does the requirement of a full and honest אֶבֶן (’even, “stone, weight”) say about faith in business?
“Do not muzzle an ox while it is treading out grain”: how does this principle apply to the way you treat those who work alongside you?
What must the Israelite bring to the priest on entering the land, and how must he present it?
Why does the confession begin with “My father was a wandering Aramean,” and what story does it sum up in a few sentences?
What does it mean to offer God the רֵאשִׁית (reshit, “firstfruits, first”), and not what is left over?
The joy of the firstfruits included the Levite and the foreigner: with whom could you share something good you have received?
What must be done with the large stones and the altar on Mount Ebal?
Why do several curses speak of what is done “in secret,” and what does it mean for the people to answer “Amen” to each one?
Whom does the series of “cursed,” with the verb אָרַר (’arar, “curse”), protect? What kind of person appears as the victim in these cases?
“Cursed is he who leads a blind man astray on the road”: what vulnerable people could you, even unintentionally, lead astray or harm?
What areas of life does the blessing reach in vv. 3-6, and how do vv. 16-19 take up these same areas?
What reason does v. 47 give for the curses, and what does the lack of joy in serving God have to do with it?
The chapter begins and ends by speaking of hearing the קוֹל (qol, “voice”) of the LORD: what does this frame suggest about the root of the blessings and curses?
The text describes a life “hanging in doubt,” fearful morning and evening: what helps you when anxiety takes the ground from under you?
Who stands before the LORD to enter the covenant, and who else is included in v. 15?
What does it mean to say that the LORD had not given them “a heart to understand” until that day?
What relationship does the chapter establish between the בְּרִית (berit, “covenant”) made at Horeb and this one made in the land of Moab?
“The secret things belong to the LORD,” but the things revealed belong to us: how does this help you deal with questions that remain unanswered?
What will happen when the people, already scattered among the nations, return to the LORD?
Why is the commandment described as near, “in your mouth and in your heart,” and how does Paul take up this text in Romans 10?
The verb שׁוּב (shuv, “return, turn back”) is repeated in the chapter: who returns and who brings back?
“So choose life”: what concrete choice before you today resembles this choice between life and death?
What does Moses command to be done with the law every seven years, and who was to be present to hear it?
Why does God order a song to be written if He already foresees the people's unfaithfulness?
Where does the strength asked of Joshua and the people with the verb חָזַק (chazaq, “be strong”) come from, according to the chapter?
“He will never leave you nor forsake you”: in what transition of your life do you need to hear this promise?
What images does the song use to describe God's care for Jacob in the wilderness?
What happens to Jeshurun when he “grew fat,” and what does he abandon at that moment?
God is called צוּר (tsur, “Rock”) several times: what does the image communicate, and with what other “rocks” is it compared in the song?
“They are not idle words for you, but they are your life”: what word of God has been life to you, and not just information?
Which tribes receive a blessing from Moses, and is any of the tribes of Israel left unmentioned?
What does the blessing of Levi highlight about that tribe's calling?
Benjamin and Israel will dwell in בֶּטַח (betach, “security”): what makes this security possible, according to the chapter?
“The eternal God is your dwelling place, and underneath are the everlasting arms”: at what moment have you needed to lean on these arms?
What does the LORD show Moses from the top of Pisgah, and what promise does He recall?
What stands out in the death and burial of Moses, and in the people's mourning?
The expression “face to face” uses the word פָּנִים (panim, “face”): how does it sum up Moses' relationship with God?
Joshua carries on the work because Moses laid his hands on him: what legacy are you passing on, and to whom?
